chapter: Not in the Yoga Sutras (Sāṃkhya vocabulary; cf. asmitā, YS 2.6)
literal_gloss: I-making; the faculty that generates the sense of self
philosophical_gloss: Ahaṃkāra is the ego-function in Sāṃkhya psychology — the faculty that appropriates experience as 'mine' and generates the sense of being a separate self. It is a product of prakṛti (not puruṣa) and is part of the 'inner instrument' (antaḥkaraṇa) alongside buddhi (intellect) and manas (thinking mind). In the Yoga Sutras, asmitā (I-am-ness) is the experiential face of ahaṃkāra.
doctrinal_significance: The ego as a constructed faculty, not an ultimate self. Understanding ahaṃkāra as a product of prakṛti is key to the Yoga Sutras' soteriology.
ambiguity_notes: Verified as absent: a search of the full Yogasūtra mūla text (GRETIL patyog_u, 195 sūtras) finds no occurrence of this word. Patañjali's nearest term is asmitā (YS 2.6), which is not simply a synonym: ahaṃkāra is the Sāṃkhya evolute that produces the sense of self, asmitā the kleśa of identifying seer with seen.

chapter: Not in the Yoga Sutras (Patañjali's term is kaivalya)
philosophical_gloss: Mokṣa is the general Indian philosophical term for liberation from the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra). Patañjali does not use the word mokṣa — he uses kaivalya ('aloneness') instead, which carries specifically Sāṃkhya-Yoga connotations. In Vedānta, mokṣa means realization of identity with Brahman. In Buddhism, liberation is nirvāṇa. Each tradition fills 'liberation' with different metaphysical content.
doctrinal_significance: The pan-Indian concept of liberation. Patañjali's kaivalya is his specific version of mokṣa.
ambiguity_notes: Verified as absent: a search of the full Yogasūtra mūla text (GRETIL patyog_u, 195 sūtras) finds no occurrence of this word. Where other systems say mokṣa, Patañjali says kaivalya ('aloneness', YS 2.25, 3.50, 3.55, 4.26, 4.34). The substitution is deliberate: liberation is the isolation of puruṣa from prakṛti, not release into union with anything. Patañjali uses kaivalya, not mokṣa. Including mokṣa here because it is the broader concept students will encounter across Indian philosophy.

chapter: Not in the Yoga Sutras (Sāṃkhya guṇa)
literal_gloss: dust; passion; the quality of activity and agitation
philosophical_gloss: Rajas is the guṇa of activity, restlessness, and passion. It drives movement, desire, and effort. Too much rajas makes the mind agitated and unable to settle. The same root (√rañj) gives us rāga (attachment) — both involve the 'coloring' of awareness by passion. Yogic practice reduces rajas through calming practices and ethical restraints.
doctrinal_significance: The guṇa of restless energy. Explains why the mind is naturally agitated and difficult to still.
ambiguity_notes: Verified as absent: a search of the full Yogasūtra mūla text (GRETIL patyog_u, 195 sūtras) finds no occurrence of this word. Patañjali refers to the guṇas as a set (YS 1.16, 2.15, 2.19) and describes them at YS 2.18 as prakāśa, kriyā and sthiti, but never names sattva, rajas and tamas as a triad. Only sattva occurs by name (YS 2.41, 3.35, 3.49, 3.55).

chapter: Not in the Yoga Sutras (Sāṃkhya guṇa)
philosophical_gloss: Tamas is the guṇa of inertia, darkness, and dullness. It produces ignorance, sleep, and resistance to change. Many of the obstacles to yoga (styāna, ālasya, nidrā) are tāmasic in nature. Yoga combats tamas through tapas (disciplined heat) and sattva-building practices. The goal is not to destroy tamas but to bring the guṇas into a balance where sattva predominates.
doctrinal_significance: The guṇa of darkness and inertia. Explains why the mind resists practice and tends toward dullness.
ambiguity_notes: Verified as absent: a search of the full Yogasūtra mūla text (GRETIL patyog_u, 195 sūtras) finds no occurrence of this word. See the note at rajas: Patañjali names the guṇas collectively and describes them at YS 2.18, but does not use the names rajas and tamas.

chapter: Not a sūtra word; the traditional title of Pāda 3

prefixes.meaning: apart, specially (here: manifesting in extraordinary ways)

suffixes.grammatical_function: forms feminine noun: 'extraordinary manifestation, supernatural power'

philosophical_gloss: Vibhūti titles the third chapter of the Yoga Sutras (Vibhūti Pāda). It refers to the special powers and attainments that arise from saṃyama — knowledge of past lives, clairvoyance, understanding of other minds, etc. These are treated as real but ultimately as distractions from the goal of kaivalya.
doctrinal_significance: Names the entire category of yogic powers. The Vibhūti Pāda catalogs them while ultimately subordinating them to liberation.
ambiguity_notes: Verified as absent: a search of the full Yogasūtra mūla text (GRETIL patyog_u, 195 sūtras) finds no occurrence of this word. Vibhūti is the name given to the third pāda in the colophons and in later tradition, not a term Patañjali uses. The powers themselves are described at YS 3.16-3.55, where the word used is siddhi.

roots.meaning: to be heavy, to raise up

suffixes.grammatical_function: forms an adjective 'heavy', used substantively as 'teacher'

philosophical_gloss: Guru means 'heavy' — the weighty one, whose gravity holds the student. Its best known statement is Muṇḍaka 1.2.12, where one who has examined the worlds won by action and grown disenchanted takes fuel in hand and approaches a teacher learned in scripture and established in brahman. That passage could not be verified in the corpus available here, so this entry is presented as a working entry rather than a checked one.
doctrinal_significance: The Upaniṣads make the teacher structurally necessary rather than merely helpful. For the verified Upaniṣadic statement of that point, see ācārya and the Gandhāra parable at ChU 6.14.2.
ambiguity_notes: Not source-verified. The Muṇḍaka and Kena Upaniṣads are absent from the GRETIL corpus consulted, and no clear occurrence was found in the eight principal Upaniṣads searched. The morphology given here follows standard dictionaries, not a checked passage.
